7th August 2026 International Coworking Day

Women didn't only join coworking. They were there when it started.

On the 9th of August 2005, the first coworking space opened its doors at Spiral Muse, a feminist collective in San Francisco. Twenty one years on, I'm picking up where they left off, and making this one about women in business, working alongside each other as the amazing collaborators we've always been.

The actual day falls on a Sunday this year, and nobody's opening their laptop on a Sunday. So I'm holding it on Friday the 7th instead.

“I think realizing that you're not alone, that you are standing with millions of your sisters around the world is vital.” Malala Yousafzai, Activist

Running a business can be a lonely thing, even when it doesn't look like it from the outside

You can have a full client list, a business that looks like it's working, and still sit down at your desk most days with no one to talk anything through with. No one who sees the actual workload behind the scenes. No one working alongside you while you get through it. That's not a small thing. It adds up.

Coworking spaces and business owners everywhere will be marking International Coworking Day, working alongside each other because so many of us do our best work in company, not in isolation. I wanted women in business to have a place inside that.

I'm doing this because I like connecting women in business. Open to every woman in business, whatever your brain does or doesn't do.

Here's the quick science of why working alongside someone else actually helps

You know the thing. It's been sitting on your list for weeks, maybe longer, and every time you sit down to do it alone, something else feels more urgent, more interesting, or more possible. That's not a character flaw. That's what happens to most brains when the only accountability in the room is the one inside your own head.

When another person is quietly working nearby, even on a screen, your brain treats it differently than working alone. It's called the social facilitation effect, and it means having someone present, even virtually, can lift your focus and your working memory. Researchers also talk about mirroring, where watching someone else stay on task makes it easier for your own brain to do the same. And having another person there gives you a bit of external structure to lean on, so you're not relying only on your own executive function to keep you at your desk.

None of that is about willpower. It's about how brains, all brains, respond to the people around them. At ADHD Village this is something I know a lot about, because it tends to matter even more for ADHD and AuDHD brains, but you don't need one of those to feel the benefit.

What actually happens on the afternoon

This isn't a workshop, and it isn't a webinar where you sit and listen. It's an actual working session, where you bring your own task and I hold the space around you while you do it.

Celebrate what got done

Bring whatever you want to get done. Invoices, that email you've been rehearsing in your head, the admin pile, a project you can't seem to start on your own. You don't need to explain yourself, and you don't need to have it together before you arrive.

When the third block finishes, I don't let everyone log off and scatter. Everyone comes back together, names what got done out loud, and celebrates it, even if what got done is smaller than what you'd planned. Finishing something deserves a moment, not a scroll straight on to the next tab.

Connection over competition

Women in business are so often told to compete with each other, for clients, for attention, for the next opportunity. This afternoon is built on the opposite idea. That you get more done, and feel less alone doing it, when you work alongside other women instead of against them. That's the whole point of the day, and it's the whole point of this session.

Hostess with the most-ess (well, people DO SAY I can be too much!)

I'm Mel, I run ADHD Village, coaching women in business who are late diagnosed ADHD or AuDHD, perimenopausal or menopausal, and worn out by systems that were never built for their brain. This is about coming back to yourself, not becoming someone new, safety before strategy, every time.

I'm AuDHD myself, late-diagnosed, twenty four years into running my own businesses, and I know what it's like to build something real while feeling like you're doing it alone. I love helping women connect, feel safe, and actually tick things off the list that's been sitting there, and if you get stuck during the coworking, I'm right there to help. I'm opening this one up to all women in business, whoever you are.
